answer.rationale: The tempting move is switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor, because memory_c2 says exactly that worked and their quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate. But that memory is the single load-bearing claim for the riskiest action, so it is the first thing I want the archive to confirm: what volume it covered, whether the switched part was on the critical path, and whether 'onboarding was quick' meant weeks or a quarter. A cheap, accurate-invoicing vendor at low volume is not evidence of a safe primary-supply cutover at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and 14 days before expiry. Migration under those conditions puts delivery risk squarely on the line that owes committed volume downstream, and the primary objective forbids buying cost with delivery risk. I also want memory_c4 verified, since renegotiation is my intended path and I need to know whether the recovered margin was a few points or something near 18% before I rely on it to meet the mandate. My current intent is to spend the single decision on negotiating at renewal with the incumbent, using the low-cost quote as documented benchmark leverage. That captures memory_c4's mechanism and memory_c6's volume pricing while preserving the integration stability of memory_c1, and it keeps the vendor relationship intact rather than burning it on a cutover I cannot de-risk this cycle. If verification shows memory_c2 was in fact a comparable-volume, critical-path switch and memory_c4's savings were trivial, I would revisit switching, but I would still want it staged rather than a wholesale cutover. Held uncertainty: I do not know if the incumbent will move 18%, and negotiation may close only part of the gap; if so the residual is a next-review problem, likely paired with memory_c3's second-source approach once there is schedule slack to absorb qualification. Deferring is unattractive here because the contract does not auto-renew, so memory_c5's month-to-month fallback may simply not exist.
